title: How the Web Works
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of how the web works in a browser document.
Apply at least one relevant rule from this lesson to a small HTML example.
Check the result using browser inspection, a validator, or an accessibility checklist.

content.intro: A web page is the result of a request, resource delivery, parsing, and rendering. Understanding that path makes local debugging and publishing less mysterious.
content.why_it_matters: A clear foundation reduces syntax mistakes later and helps you read other people’s markup without treating it as mysterious code.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: What a website and web page are is one of the decisions covered by How the Web Works. Decide what the markup is meant to communicate, choose the native HTML structure that expresses that meaning, and verify the result in a browser or a relevant validation checklist. Avoid using an element or attribute just because its default appearance seems convenient.

items.title: How browsers display web pages
items.text: Browsers parse HTML into a document tree and recover from many authoring errors. Browser recovery is not a substitute for valid markup; inspect the DOM and validate the original source.

items.title: How HTML, CSS, and JavaScript work together
items.text: Keep responsibilities distinct: HTML supplies meaning and structure, CSS controls visual presentation, and JavaScript adds behavior. A page can use all three without confusing their roles.

content_blocks.title: Keep in mind
content_blocks.text: Prefer the native semantic element that communicates intent. Do not choose markup solely for its default visual style.

content.task: Create a small HTML example that demonstrates how the web works. Keep the markup minimal, give every element a clear purpose, and inspect the rendered result.
task_acceptance_criteria: Use the relevant concept from How the Web Works.
Keep IDs unique and use valid nesting.
Check the result in a browser and record one finding.
hints: Start with the smallest valid example for how the web works.
Add one element or attribute at a time, then check the result.
Compare the source and rendered DOM if the behavior surprises you.
content.expected_output: The HTML displays the button and hidden paragraph. The external JavaScript file must exist to change the paragraph on activation.

troubleshooting.symptom: The expected content does not appear.
troubleshooting.check: Confirm the file was saved with an .html extension and inspect its path and nesting.
Check the resolved URL and confirm the referenced file or external resource exists and allows the request.

troubleshooting.symptom: The page looks correct but the markup may be invalid.
troubleshooting.check: Run the Nu Html Checker and follow its first relevant diagnostic, then validate again.

common_mistakes.why: The default appearance is not the element’s main meaning and can make navigation or maintenance harder.
common_mistakes.fix: Choose the element that matches the content purpose, then use CSS for presentation.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a browser’s recovery means the source is valid
common_mistakes.why: Browsers often recover from malformed markup, which can hide defects and produce unexpected document structure.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect the rendered DOM and run a validator against the original source.

common_mistakes.why: Missing files, narrow viewports, keyboard access, invalid input, or other states can expose defects.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected state plus one realistic edge case and an accessibility path.

summary: How the Web Works is about expressing document structure or behavior intentionally.

Static pages versus dynamically generated pages is one of the decisions covered by How the Web Works. Decide what the markup is meant to communicate, choose the native HTML structure that expresses that meaning, and verify the result in a browser or a relevant validation checklist. Avoid using an element or attribute just because its default appearance seems convenient.
Verify both markup and behavior; do not infer correctness from appearance alone.
